title: Whiteman visits Atlantic City and conducts the Goldkette band
summary: Whiteman, Busse, the Rhythm Boys and Malneck drove down; Whiteman led the band in St. Louis Blues to huge applause as Goldkette arrived.

story.theme_name: Working with and around Louis Armstrong
story.community_name: Playing with and around Louis Armstrong

blocks.x: So anyway, we were playing at the Pier down there -- this was the -- was it the Steel or the Million Dollar Pier, that's often confused, said Steel Pier, but I think it's the Million Dollar Pier. The band is doing very well, as far as that's concerned, but no tremendous crowds down there. So one night we're around there and who walks in but Jimmy. Now, Jimmy had made several of our recording dates and all the guys knew him anyway and liked him, but he comes in this one night and he's bringing Paul Whiteman, and he's bringing Henry Busse and he's got Bing and the other Rhythm Boys, Barris and Rinker and let's see, he's got Matty Malneck was there. Well, he
had quite a bit and he had talked them all into driving down. I guess he had talked Paul into driving them down --

From Philadelphia. They were appearing in Philadelphia at a theatre and I guess after the last show they came down, had enough time. We were very happy to see them, of course, and it was an event. So we got talking between sets and Bix and I went over to Paul and said, 'Why don't you come up on the stand, and conduct the band?' 'I don't know any of the arrangements,' he said. 'You don't have to know the arrangements, beat lead off and the band plays, that's all.' Okay.

He comes up on the stand and he goes off, in the way -- Lawrence Welk all over, a-one and a-two, you know, I think that's where Welk got it. But he used to clown around a lot and he starts that off, 'What will we play?' so they start off with something, I forget, I think it was a thing called 'Sorry,' where the band starts off like a shotgun. Chauncey used to start it off with a revolver, bang, on a rimshot and it was one of Quicksell's tunes.

Well, they get started on that, he's up there and as soon as he's there, it seemed like we had a hell of a crowd. They came from all over and they gather around the stand, which pointed out that this is what our band needed all the time, somebody to stand up.

Right, somebody to make the announcements, somebody to sing, somebody to do something. We had guys to sing, and Frankie was in front of the band, but it wasn't the same thing. You could tell when he was up there, he was just standing up, where with Whiteman there's so much presence there that these are my boys, that sort of thing. You don't get that with the other guys. But anyway, the people gather around then he turns around and talks to them. "What do you want to hear?" Well, I can almost tell in his mind what the next tune is going to be, "St. Louis Blues" or one of those things. He didn't care what they said they wanted to hear, he was going to play St. Louis Blues and this is what he did, he turned around and said "Okay," and whatever the guys said out there, or one of them, he'd pick one out and turn around and then they started and the guys right away, if there was any tune they hated to play it was "St. Louis Blues" and you know how you get requests for "St. Louis Blues," in those days at least.

And they started off playing it in such a corny way, (Sings), they started going like that until they realized there's Paul up there and let's not make a fool out of him because actually it was his decision. He made "St. Louis Blues" and this is something we never played. Then they played it and you know, it was faked mostly, and they played it very well. Beautifully, in fact, and at the end of it, of course, this "St. Louis Blues," the applause we got it was tremendous. The
band never got applause like that. What else happened, I suppose, I don't know whether I should say this, but who's standing down at the door just came in, was Jean.
